2.2: How did Akka achieve these results?
3.1: Hyperscalers charge for consumption: every request, token and trace adds to the bill, so cost grows with success and is hard to forecast. Akka charges a flat annual fee, known in advance, and extra use adds only the hardware it runs on.
4.1: Akka runs the whole stack on the lowest-priced hardware: compute, storage and network. Inference, AI controls, model routing, small language model training, agent execution, memory, workflows, messaging, gateway, governance, observability and evaluation all run there. Hyperscalers take their margin above that layer, on metered managed services: agent runtime, memory, gateway, observability, evaluation and policy, each billed by the unit. That is most of the bill.
5.1: Interpreted languages carry a memory overhead for every session, and their concurrency models limit how many run on a node. Akka runs each session as a small actor, so one node holds many waiting sessions. Sessions, agents, evaluations, guardrails, workflows, endpoints, data queries and timers all run as actors. A cluster spreads them by key and rebalances when a node leaves. No state is lost, and the sessions continue.
6.1: Assembled frameworks are allocated and managed separately, each keeping its own headroom, which is paid for and unused. In Akka, everything that runs as an actor shares one compute model: agents, evaluations, guardrails, workflows, endpoints, data queries and timers draw on one pool, so capacity goes to whichever part needs it.
6.2: Akka’s memory uses event-sourced entities: every change is recorded in a journal, and all data is cached in memory. A system recovers from the journal, runs active in two regions at once with a short recovery time and recovery point, and reads and writes AI memory in low single-digit milliseconds.
7.1: Hyperscalers sell these functions as separate products, each its own layer, and the customer pays to wire them together. Akka ships the whole stack as one piece, already joined, including training, agent execution and memory. No licences to retain for event streaming, a cache, messaging, workflow orchestration, a gateway, AI governance, observability, evaluation or red teaming.
8.1: Model spend is its own cost area. Cost per token moves with volume, model mix, prompt size, cache use, response size and price. The console finds avoidable cost: prompts that skip the cache, failed attempts, duplicate requests, reasoning above the median, unused tool definitions, answers longer than needed. A cheaper model is proposed only when it meets the owner’s quality bar, and the ledger keeps the estimated saving beside what was measured. Over six months, Akka’s own cost per token fell seventy-three percent.
9.1: Specify accepts requirements as they already exist: hand drawings, spreadsheets, issue lists and broad descriptions. Engineers, ML engineers, product managers, analysts and executives all take part in writing the specification. The people who know the business contribute to the system directly. Each requirement is captured by whoever holds it, so fewer handoffs sit between the business and the engineer.
9.2: Specify builds every system on a standard architecture from a specification that holds its purpose, exit conditions and definition of done. Every system is built the same way, so it can be read the same way, and what it is for is written in the specification. An engineer who has never seen a system finds its purpose in the specification, not in the code.
9.3: When a key engineer leaves, the knowledge stays with the system. Akka’s context holds current best practice, and Specify re-aligns existing systems as it changes, so technical debt does not build up. Fewer engineers maintain more systems.
